claims.text: The initial TiVNbTa alloy is a single-phase BCC alloy with a dendritic microstructure.
The initial TiVNbTa alloy has a yield strength of approximately 800 MPa at lower temperatures.
The unmodified TiVNbTa alloy has a yield strength of approximately 330 MPa at 1273 K.
The unmodified TiVNbTa alloy has a compressive strength of 423 MPa at 30% strain and 1273 K.
A small carbon addition followed by heat treatment will form TiC precipitates within the BCC TiVNbTa matrix.
The resulting TiC precipitates will be nanoscale and uniformly distributed in the BCC matrix.
The TiC precipitates will remain stable at elevated temperature.
TiC precipitates will obstruct and pin dislocations, producing precipitation hardening.
Dislocation obstruction by the carbides will retard thermally activated softening at 1273 K.
The carbon-modified alloy will have significantly higher yield strength at 1273 K than the unmodified 330 MPa baseline.
The carbon-modified alloy will have significantly higher compressive strength at 1273 K than the unmodified 423 MPa baseline.
The elevated-temperature strengths could approach the alloy's low-temperature performance.
The proposed operating boundary is continuous service at or near 1273 K.
The proposed mechanical boundary includes compressive strains around 30% under loads representative of a W/CuCrZr intermediate layer.
Carbon addition could cause embrittlement or reduced toughness if its concentration or the precipitate distribution is unsuitable.
Failure to improve both yield strength and compressive strength by more than 20% at 1273 K relative to an identically processed carbon-free control would falsify the hypothesis.
Embrittlement or abnormal microstructural degradation in the carbon-added samples would falsify the hypothesis.
